title: CBC, blood smear and anemia classification
covers: How blood cells are made, what a complete blood count and a smear tell you, how anemia is defined (WHO 2024) and classified, and the first steps of the work-up.

items.p: A stem cell gives a myeloid and a lymphoid line. Growth factors steer each lineage.

ul: Red cells: erythropoietin (kidney; rises with hypoxia and anemia)
Platelets: thrombopoietin
Neutrophils: G-CSF. Eosinophils: IL-5. Basophils: IL-3. Monocytes: M-CSF.

items.p: Red cell precursors mature in the marrow for about 5 days. Their cytoplasm turns from blue (RNA) to pink (hemoglobin) and the nucleus is expelled. The reticulocyte spends 1–2 days in blood; the mature cell lives 120 days.
Iron is needed for hemoglobin; B12 and folate for DNA.

table: Average red cell size; the most useful index

ul: Hematocrit is roughly 3 × hemoglobin
In children the lower limit of MCV is about 70 + age in years
White cells 4.5–11 × 10⁹/L: neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 1–6%, basophils under 2%
Platelets 150–450 × 10⁹/L; lifespan 7–10 days

items.p: Four globin chains, each with a heme (iron in protoporphyrin IX) that binds one oxygen molecule.

ul: α genes: chromosome 16. β genes: chromosome 11.
HbF = α2γ2. HbA = α2β2. HbA2 = α2δ2.
The γ-to-β switch happens around birth, so β-chain diseases appear after about 6 months

items.p: The reticulocyte count shows what the marrow is doing. It is the best single test to separate failed production from destruction or loss.

ul: High: bleeding or hemolysis
Low or "normal" despite anemia: marrow failure or ineffective erythropoiesis
Ret-He: early sign of iron-restricted red cell production

items.p: Read where cells just touch (the monolayer). Bluish cells (polychromasia) mean many reticulocytes.

table: Thalassemia, liver disease, HbC, after splenectomy
HUS, TTP, DIC, mechanical heart valve
Hemolysis, marrow stress; normal in newborns

items.p: Anemia is a hemoglobin more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, adjusted for altitude and smoking.
Severe anemia is below 7.0 in children under 5 and in pregnancy, and below 8.0 otherwise. Iron deficiency is the leading cause worldwide.
Use mechanism (less production, destruction, loss) and cell size together.

ul: Microcytic (MCV under 80): iron deficiency, thalassemia, late anemia of inflammation, lead, sideroblastic anemia
Normocytic: use reticulocytes. Low: marrow failure. High: bleeding or hemolysis. Normal: early anemia of inflammation.
Macrocytic (MCV over 100): megaloblastic (B12, folate, drugs) or not (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia)
Confirm anemia with the right threshold
History: diet, bleeding, jaundice, drugs, lead, family (early gallbladder or spleen removal suggests hemolysis)
Examination: pallor, jaundice, bleeding, large liver, spleen or nodes
Simple tests: CBC with indices, reticulocyte count, smear

items.p: Slow-onset anemia can be well tolerated even at a very low hemoglobin.
Without inflammation: ferritin 20 ng/mL or less in children, 30 or less in adults. With inflammation in adults: ferritin under 100 or transferrin saturation under 20%.
The lecture case: a 4-year-old on cow's milk, Hb 6.0, MCV 70. Severe microcytic anemia from iron deficiency. Oral iron brings reticulocytes up within a week.

cards.q: Where is erythropoietin made, and what raises it?
cards.a: Mainly the kidney; hypoxia and anemia

cards.q: Lifespan of red cells, reticulocytes in blood, and platelets
cards.a: 120 days; 1–2 days; 7–10 days

cards.q: MCV: normal range and child's lower limit
cards.a: 80–100 fL; in children about 70 + age in years
Variation in red cell size (anisocytosis); normal 12–15%
About 3 × hemoglobin
α on chromosome 16; β on chromosome 11

cards.q: Composition of HbA, HbA2 and HbF
cards.a: HbA α2β2; HbA2 α2δ2; HbF α2γ2

cards.q: Why do β-chain disorders show after 6 months?
cards.a: The γ-to-β switch occurs around birth, so HbF protects early on.

cards.q: Most informative test to tell production failure from destruction
cards.a: Reticulocyte count
Reticulocytosis
Microangiopathic hemolysis (HUS, TTP, DIC) or a mechanical heart valve
G6PD deficiency or other oxidant hemolysis
Thalassemia, liver disease, HbC, after splenectomy
Hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis
Marrow fibrosis or infiltration (also thalassemia)
Hb more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex, adjusted for altitude and smoking

cards.q: WHO 2024 anemia cutoffs: 6–23 months, 24–59 months, 5–11 years
WHO 2024 anemia cutoffs: women, men, pregnancy
cards.a: Women 12.0; men 13.0; pregnancy 11.0 (10.5 in the 2nd trimester)
Iron deficiency, thalassemia, late anemia of inflammation, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia
Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, drugs
Hemorrhage or hemolysis
Children ≤ 20 ng/mL; adults ≤ 30 ng/mL
Ferritin < 100 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%

cards.q: First sign of response to oral iron
cards.a: Reticulocytosis within about a week

questions.stem: Which growth factor is matched with the lineage it steers?

options.A: IL-5: basophils; IL-15: T cells
options.B: IL-3: eosinophils; IL-7: NK cells
options.C: IL-5: eosinophils; IL-15: NK cells
options.D: G-CSF: monocytes; M-CSF: neutrophils
options.E: TPO: red cells; EPO: platelets

questions.explanation: EPO red cells, TPO platelets, G-CSF neutrophils, IL-5 eosinophils, IL-3 basophils, M-CSF monocytes, IL-7 B and T cells, IL-15 NK cells. A: Basophils are steered by IL-3 and T cells by IL-7. B: IL-3 is for basophils and IL-7 for B and T cells. D: Reversed. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: Which sequence of erythropoiesis is correct?

options.A: Proerythroblast, polychromatic, basophilic, orthochromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte
options.B: Proerythroblast, basophilic, orthochromatic, polychromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte
options.C: Reticulocyte, proerythroblast, basophilic, polychromatic, orthochromatic erythroblast
options.D: Proerythroblast, basophilic, polychromatic, orthochromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte
options.E: Basophilic, proerythroblast, polychromatic, orthochromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte

questions.explanation: Proerythroblast, basophilic erythroblast, polychromatic erythroblast, orthochromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte, mature red cell. A: Basophilic precedes polychromatic. B: Polychromatic precedes orthochromatic. C: The reticulocyte comes last before the mature cell. E: The proerythroblast comes first.

questions.stem: How long does each stage of a red cell's life last?

options.A: Marrow about 1–2 days; reticulocyte in blood 5 days; mature cell 120 days
options.B: Marrow about 5 days; reticulocyte in blood 1–2 days; mature cell 120 days
options.C: Marrow about 5 days; reticulocyte in blood 7–10 days; mature cell 120 days
options.D: Marrow about 5 days; reticulocyte in blood 1–2 days; mature cell 60 days
options.E: Marrow about 15 days; reticulocyte in blood 1–2 hours; mature cell 100 days

questions.explanation: Bone marrow about 5 days, reticulocyte in blood 1–2 days, mature red cell 120 days; about 1% of red cells are replaced daily. A: The first two are swapped. C: 7–10 days is the platelet lifespan. D: The lifespan is 120 days. E: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: Why does the cytoplasm of red cell precursors change colour as they mature?

options.A: Blue RNA and ribosomes are replaced by pink hemoglobin
options.B: Pink RNA and ribosomes are replaced by blue hemoglobin
options.C: The nucleus is extruded, leaving a blue cytoplasm
options.D: Iron accumulates and stains the cytoplasm blue
options.E: Mitochondria multiply and stain the cytoplasm pink

questions.explanation: Cytoplasm shifts from blue (RNA, ribosomes) to pink (hemoglobin) as the cell matures; the nucleus condenses and is then extruded. B: The colours are swapped. C: Nuclear extrusion does not explain the colour shift. D: Not the explanation given. E: Not the explanation given.

questions.stem: Which statement about erythropoietin is correct?

options.A: Made mainly by the liver; rises with hypoxia and anemia
options.B: Made mainly by the kidney; falls with hypoxia and anemia
options.C: Made mainly by the marrow; rises with iron overload
options.D: Made mainly by the spleen; rises with polycythemia
options.E: Made mainly by the kidney; rises with hypoxia and anemia

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is made mainly by the kidney; it rises with hypoxia and anemia and drives red cell production and release. A: The main source is the kidney. B: It rises. C: Not as described. D: Not as described.

questions.stem: Which factors does the lecture give for normal erythropoiesis, apart from erythropoietin?

options.A: Iron for DNA; B12 and folate for hemoglobin; thyroxine and testosterone accelerate it
options.B: Iron for hemoglobin; B12 and folate for DNA; cortisol and estrogen accelerate it
options.C: Copper for hemoglobin; vitamin K for DNA; insulin accelerates it
options.D: Iron for hemoglobin; B12 and folate for DNA; thyroxine and testosterone accelerate it
options.E: Iron for hemoglobin; vitamin C and zinc for DNA; thyroxine slows it

questions.explanation: Iron is needed for hemoglobin, B12 and folate for DNA; thyroxine and testosterone accelerate erythropoiesis. A: Roles of iron and vitamins are swapped. B: The hormones named are thyroxine and testosterone. C: Not the factors given. E: Not the factors given.

questions.stem: What must an ageing red cell retain to keep circulating, and what removes it when this is lost?

options.A: It must keep its nucleus to pass the spleen; neutrophils remove old cells
options.B: It must stay deformable to pass the spleen; macrophages remove old cells
options.C: It must stay rigid to resist the spleen; complement lyses old cells
options.D: It must keep its ribosomes; the liver filters old cells
options.E: It must stay deformable to pass the kidney; podocytes remove old cells

questions.explanation: Cells must stay deformable to pass the spleen; macrophages remove old cells. A: Mature red cells have no nucleus, and macrophages remove them. C: Deformability is required. D: Not as described. E: The spleen and macrophages are named.

questions.stem: Which statement about the complete blood count is correct?

options.A: The reticulocyte count is part of each differential
options.B: The differential lists red cell indices
options.C: The reticulocyte count is reported on request
options.D: MPV is a red cell index
options.E: RDW describes variation in platelet size

questions.explanation: CBC: red cell count, Hb/hematocrit, indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW), reticulocyte count on request; white cell count and differential; platelet count and MPV. A: It is on request. B: The differential lists white cell types. D: MPV is mean platelet volume. E: RDW concerns red cells.

questions.stem: Normal CBC values depend on age and sex. On which additional factors does hemoglobin depend (WHO 2024)?

options.A: Altitude and ethnicity
options.B: Smoking and inflammation
options.C: Body weight and diet
options.D: Ethnicity and inflammation
options.E: Altitude and smoking

questions.explanation: Normal values depend on age and sex, and hemoglobin also on altitude and smoking. A: WHO 2024 makes no adjustment for ethnicity. B: No adjustment for inflammation. C: Not listed. D: Neither is adjusted for.

questions.stem: Which description of the mature red cell is correct?

options.A: A 7–8 µm biconcave disc without nucleus or mitochondria
options.B: A 7–8 µm biconcave disc with mitochondria but no nucleus
options.C: A 12–15 µm sphere without nucleus or ribosomes
options.D: A 2–3 µm disc with a small surface-to-volume ratio
options.E: A 7–8 µm biconcave disc that divides in the circulation

questions.explanation: Red cells are flexible 7–8 µm biconcave discs with a large surface-to-volume ratio, about 5 million/µL, lifespan 120 days, with no nucleus, ribosomes or mitochondria. B: Mitochondria are absent. C: Size and shape are wrong. D: Size is 7–8 µm and the ratio is large. E: It cannot divide or make protein.

questions.stem: Which statement about hemoglobin is correct?

options.A: About 270 million molecules per red cell; each heme (iron + protoporphyrin IX) binds four O₂
options.B: About 27,000 molecules per red cell; each globin binds one O₂ directly
options.C: About 270 million molecules per red cell; two globin chains carry one shared heme
options.D: About 2.7 billion molecules per red cell; heme is copper + protoporphyrin IX
options.E: About 270 million molecules per red cell; each heme (iron + protoporphyrin IX) binds one O₂

questions.explanation: About 270 million Hb molecules per red cell; 4 globin chains (2 α + 2 non-α), each carrying a heme group (iron + protoporphyrin IX); each heme reversibly binds one O₂. A: Each heme binds one O₂. B: Number and binding site are wrong. C: There are four chains, each with a heme. D: Heme contains iron.

questions.stem: How is hematocrit defined, and how does it relate to hemoglobin?

options.A: Percentage of blood volume occupied by plasma; about 3 × Hb
options.B: Percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells; about Hb ÷ 3
options.C: Average hemoglobin concentration in red cells; about 3 × Hb
options.D: Percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells; about 3 × Hb
options.E: Number of red cells per microliter; about 10 × Hb

questions.explanation: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells, approximately 3 × Hb. Adult Hb: males 13.5–18 g/dL, females 12–15 g/dL. A: It is the red cell fraction. B: It is about three times the Hb. C: That is the MCHC. E: Not the definition.

questions.stem: Where are the globin gene clusters located?

options.A: α cluster on chromosome 11; β cluster on chromosome 16
options.B: α cluster on chromosome 6; β cluster on chromosome 15
options.C: α cluster on chromosome 16; β cluster on chromosome 11
options.D: α and β clusters both on chromosome 16
options.E: α cluster on chromosome 14; β cluster on chromosome 22

questions.explanation: Chromosome 16: α-globin cluster (ζ, α2, α1). Chromosome 11: β-globin cluster (ε, Gγ, Aγ, δ, β). A: Reversed. B: Not the globin loci. D: The β cluster is on chromosome 11. E: Not the globin loci.

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin is matched with its composition or stage?

options.A: HbA2: α2γ2; Gower and Portland: fetal
options.B: HbA2: α2δ2; Gower, Portland: embryonic
options.C: HbF: α2δ2; HbA: α2β2
options.D: HbA: α2γ2; HbF: α2β2
options.E: HbA2: α2β2; HbA: α2δ2

questions.explanation: Embryonic Hb Gower 1, Gower 2, Portland; fetal HbF (α2γ2); adult HbA (α2β2) and HbA2 (α2δ2). A: α2γ2 is HbF, and Gower/Portland are embryonic. C: HbF is α2γ2. D: Reversed. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: Why do β-chain disorders become apparent only after about 6 months of age?

options.A: The γ-to-β switch occurs around birth
options.B: The ζ-to-α switch occurs around birth
options.C: Maternal hemoglobin persists for 6 months
options.D: The δ-to-β switch occurs at 6 months
options.E: Erythropoietin is absent until 6 months

questions.explanation: The γ-to-β switch around birth explains why β-chain disorders appear after about 6 months, as HbF declines. B: That switch is embryonic. C: Not the explanation. D: Not the explanation. E: Not the explanation.

questions.stem: Which red cell index is matched with its meaning?

options.A: RDW: average red cell volume; MCHC: variation in red cell size
options.B: MCH: average Hb concentration; MCHC: average weight of Hb per cell
options.C: MCV: variation in red cell size; RDW: average red cell volume
options.D: RDW: variation in red cell size; MCHC: average Hb concentration
options.E: MCH: average red cell volume; MCV: average weight of Hb per cell

questions.explanation: MCV 80–100 fL (average volume, most useful). RDW 12–15% (anisocytosis). MCH 27–31 pg (weight of Hb per cell). MCHC 32–36 g/dL (Hb concentration in red cells). A: Average volume is the MCV. B: Reversed. C: Reversed. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has an MCV of 70 fL. Using the lecture's rule, what is the lower limit of normal, and how is the MCV classified?

options.A: About 80 fL (adult limit); microcytic
options.B: About 66 fL (70 − age); normocytic
options.C: About 74 fL (70 + age); microcytic
options.D: About 74 fL (70 + age); normocytic
options.E: About 70 fL (fixed); normocytic

questions.explanation: In children the lower limit of normal MCV is about 70 + age (years) fL until about 80 fL: for a 4-year-old about 74 fL, so 70 fL is microcytic. A: In children the age-specific limit is used. B: The rule is 70 + age. D: 70 is below 74. E: The limit rises with age.

questions.stem: How does the reticulocyte count behave in different anemias?

options.A: High in blood loss and hemolysis; inappropriately normal or low in marrow failure
options.B: Low in blood loss and hemolysis; inappropriately high or normal in marrow failure
options.C: Increased in marrow failure and hemolysis; decreased in blood loss
options.D: Normal in hemolysis; increased in ineffective erythropoiesis
options.E: Increased in each anemia, in proportion to severity

questions.explanation: Reticulocytes (immature, non-nucleated red cells with RNA) show marrow activity: increased in blood loss and hemolysis; decreased or inappropriately normal in marrow failure and ineffective erythropoiesis. B: Reversed. C: Marrow failure lowers it. D: Hemolysis raises it; ineffective erythropoiesis does not. E: It is low when production fails.

questions.stem: What do the modern reticulocyte parameters indicate?

options.A: Ret-He: earliest marrow recovery; immature reticulocyte fraction: early iron-restricted erythropoiesis
options.B: Ret-He: early iron-restricted erythropoiesis; immature reticulocyte fraction: earliest marrow recovery
options.C: Ret-He: degree of hemolysis; immature reticulocyte fraction: B12 deficiency
options.D: Ret-He: red cell size variation; immature reticulocyte fraction: platelet turnover
options.E: Ret-He: marrow fibrosis; immature reticulocyte fraction: iron overload

questions.explanation: Reticulocyte Hb content (CHr/Ret-He) is an early marker of iron-restricted erythropoiesis; the immature reticulocyte fraction (IRF) is the earliest sign of marrow recovery. A: Reversed. C: Not the meanings given. D: Not the meanings given. E: Not the meanings given.

questions.stem: Which white cell type predominates in the blood of young children and of adults?

options.A: Neutrophils predominate in young children; lymphocytes in adults
options.B: Monocytes predominate in young children; neutrophils in adults
options.C: Lymphocytes predominate at both ages
options.D: Neutrophils predominate at both ages
options.E: Lymphocytes predominate in young children; neutrophils in adults

questions.explanation: Normal WBC count is 4.5–11.0 × 10⁹/L; lifespan from a few hours to about 15 days. Lymphocytes predominate in young children, neutrophils in adults. A: Reversed. B: Not as stated. C: Neutrophils predominate in adults. D: Lymphocytes predominate in young children.

questions.stem: Which adult differential count is normal?

options.A: Neutrophils 20–40%, lymphocytes 40–70%, monocytes 3–8%
options.B: Neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 3–8%, monocytes 20–40%
options.C: Neutrophils 70–90%, lymphocytes 5–10%, monocytes 1–2%
options.D: Neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 3–8%
options.E: Neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 10–15%

questions.explanation: Neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 1–6%, basophils under 2%. A: The first two are swapped. B: Lymphocytes and monocytes are swapped. C: Not the ranges given. E: Monocytes are 3–8%.

questions.stem: In which condition are basophils increased, according to the white cell overview?

options.A: Parasitic and helminth infections
options.B: Bacterial infections
options.C: Myeloproliferative neoplasms
options.D: Viral infections
options.E: Iron deficiency

questions.explanation: Basophils release histamine and heparin, take part in hypersensitivity and are increased in myeloproliferative neoplasms. Eosinophils rise in allergy, parasites and some cancers. A: That is listed for eosinophils. B: Neutrophils are the first-line defense. D: Not listed for basophils. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about platelets is correct?

options.A: Fragments of megakaryocyte nuclei; lifespan 7–10 days; regulated by thrombopoietin
options.B: Fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; lifespan 7–10 days; regulated by thrombopoietin
options.C: Fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; lifespan 120 days; regulated by erythropoietin
options.D: Small nucleated cells; lifespan 1–2 days; regulated by G-CSF
options.E: Fragments of monocyte cytoplasm; lifespan 7–10 days; regulated by M-CSF

questions.explanation: Platelets (150–450 × 10⁹/L, lifespan 7–10 days) are produced by fragmentation of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; they are small and non-nucleated; production is regulated by thrombopoietin. A: They come from cytoplasm and have no nucleus. C: Lifespan and hormone are wrong. D: They are non-nucleated. E: The parent cell is the megakaryocyte.

questions.stem: What does polychromasia on a blood smear indicate?

options.A: Iron deficiency
options.B: Marrow fibrosis
options.C: A smear made too thick
options.D: Oxidant hemolysis
options.E: Reticulocytosis

questions.explanation: Polychromasia: bluish-grey red cells reflecting reticulocytosis. A: Not what polychromasia reflects. B: That is suggested by teardrop cells. C: Not what polychromasia reflects. D: That is suggested by bite cells.

questions.stem: Which area of a blood smear should be read?

options.A: The monolayer, where cells just touch and pallor is visible
options.B: The thick end, where cells overlap and morphology is concentrated
options.C: The thin end, where cells are flattened and pallor is lost
options.D: Any area, since morphology is uniform along the slide
options.E: The edges, where white cells are spread out

questions.explanation: Read in the monolayer: cells just touch and central pallor is visible. Too thick: cells overlap. Too thin: cells flattened, pallor lost. B: Overlap hides morphology. C: Too thin. D: It is not uniform. E: Not the area recommended.

questions.stem: Which red cell form is matched with a setting in which it is seen?

options.A: Teardrop cell: G6PD deficiency
options.B: Target cell: hereditary spherocytosis
options.C: Nucleated red cell: mechanical heart valves
options.D: Teardrop cell: marrow fibrosis or infiltration
options.E: Sickle cell: liver disease

questions.explanation: Nucleated red cells: hemolysis, marrow stress or infiltration (normal in newborns). Teardrop cells: marrow fibrosis or infiltration, thalassemia. Sickle cells: sickle cell disease. Target cells: thalassemia, liver disease, HbC, after splenectomy. A: That is the bite cell. B: Spherocytes are seen there. C: Schistocytes are seen there. E: Target cells are seen there.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a cause of target cells EXCEPT:

options.A: Iron deficiency
options.B: Thalassemia
options.C: Liver disease
options.D: Hemoglobin C
options.E: Splenectomy

questions.explanation: Target cells (codocytes) are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, HbC and after splenectomy. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: In which genotypes does the lecture say sickle cells (drepanocytes) are seen?

options.A: HbSS, HbAS and HbCC
options.B: HbSC, HbCC and β-thalassemia major
options.C: HbSS, HbSC and HbS/β-thalassemia
options.D: HbSS exclusively
options.E: HbAS, HbAC and HbS/β-thalassemia

questions.explanation: Sickle cells: sickle cell disease (HbSS, HbSC, HbS/β-thalassemia). A: Not the list given. B: Not the list given. D: Compound states are also listed. E: Not the list given.

questions.stem: A smear shows small, dense red cells without central pallor. Which cell is this, and in which conditions is it seen?

options.A: Spherocyte; iron deficiency and thalassemia
options.B: Spherocyte; hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis
options.C: Schistocyte; hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis
options.D: Target cell; liver disease and splenectomy
options.E: Elliptocyte; hereditary elliptocytosis

questions.explanation: Spherocyte: small and dense, no central pallor; hereditary spherocytosis, immune hemolysis. A: These give hypochromic microcytes. C: Schistocytes are fragments. D: Target cells have a central dot. E: Elliptocytes are oval.

questions.stem: In which condition are pencil cells seen?

options.A: Hereditary spherocytosis
options.B: G6PD deficiency
options.C: Microangiopathic hemolysis
options.D: Marrow fibrosis
options.E: Iron deficiency

questions.explanation: Elliptocytes (ovalocytes) are seen in hereditary elliptocytosis; pencil cells in iron deficiency. A: Spherocytes are seen. B: Bite cells are seen. C: Schistocytes are seen. D: Teardrop cells are seen.

questions.stem: A patient becomes jaundiced after taking an oxidant drug; the smear shows red cells with a bite-shaped defect at the edge. Which diagnosis is suggested?

options.A: G6PD deficiency
options.B: Hereditary spherocytosis
options.C: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
options.D: Sickle cell disease
options.E: Thalassemia

questions.explanation: Bite cells (degmacytes) are seen in G6PD deficiency and other oxidant hemolysis. B: Spherocytes would be seen. C: Schistocytes would be seen. D: Sickle cells would be seen. E: Target and teardrop cells would be seen.

questions.stem: In which settings are schistocytes seen?

options.A: HUS, TTP, liver disease and splenectomy
options.B: HUS, TTP, DIC and mechanical heart valves
options.C: Hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis
options.D: G6PD deficiency and other oxidant hemolysis
options.E: Marrow fibrosis and thalassemia

questions.explanation: Schistocytes (helmet and triangle fragments) are seen in microangiopathic hemolysis (HUS, TTP, DIC) and with mechanical heart valves. A: The last two give target cells. C: These give spherocytes. D: These give bite cells. E: These give teardrop cells.

questions.stem: What does the lecture conclude about AI tools such as CytoDiffusion in smear review?

options.A: A replacement for the clinician once sensitivity exceeds 0.9
options.B: A tool no better than chance at detecting unseen blasts
options.C: A second reader that does not replace the clinician
options.D: A tool validated for routine use in diverse populations
options.E: A tool that cannot explain which image regions drive its calls

questions.explanation: CytoDiffusion (2025) reached 0.91 sensitivity for unseen abnormal cells at 0.96 specificity (0.28 for a standard classifier). It flags uncertain cells and shows heat maps; it does not replace the clinician and needs further testing. A: It does not replace reading the smear in clinical context. B: That describes the standard vision-transformer classifier (0.28). D: It still needs testing in diverse populations. E: It shows heat maps.

questions.stem: How is anemia defined?

options.A: Hb more than 1 SD below the mean for age and sex, adjusted for ethnicity
options.B: Hb below 12 g/dL at any age
options.C: Hematocrit more than 2 SD below the mean, adjusted for weight
options.D: Red cell count below 4 million/µL, adjusted for altitude
options.E: Hb more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex

questions.explanation: Anemia: hemoglobin more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex in a healthy reference population, adjusted for altitude and smoking. It is the most common blood disorder worldwide. A: The definition uses 2 SD and no ethnicity adjustment. B: Thresholds vary with age and sex. C: The definition uses Hb. D: The definition uses Hb.

questions.stem: Which example shows that hemoglobin must be read in context?

options.A: Hb 14 g/dL is normal in any 2-year-old
options.B: Hb 7.5 g/dL means severe anemia in a 2-month-old preterm infant
options.C: Hb 11 g/dL means anemia in a second-trimester pregnancy
options.D: Hb 14 g/dL can mean anemia with cyanotic heart disease
options.E: Hb 12.5 g/dL is normal in an adult man

questions.explanation: Hb 7.5 g/dL can be normal for age in a 2-month-old preterm infant (physiologic nadir); Hb 14 g/dL can mean anemia in a 2-year-old with cyanotic heart disease. A: Not with cyanotic heart disease. B: It can be the physiologic nadir. C: The cutoff there is 10.5. E: The cutoff for men is 13.0.

questions.stem: Which statement about the global burden of anemia is correct?

options.A: 1.92 billion people (24.3%) in 2021; malaria is the leading cause
options.B: 192 million people (2.4%) in 2021; dietary iron deficiency is the leading cause
options.C: 1.92 billion people (28.2%) in 2021, up from 24.3% in 1990
options.D: 3.9 billion people (48%) in 2021; B12 deficiency is the leading cause
options.E: 1.92 billion people (24.3%) in 2021; dietary iron deficiency is the leading cause

questions.explanation: 1.92 billion people had anemia in 2021 (24.3%, down from 28.2% in 1990). Dietary iron deficiency leads all causes. Most affected: children under 5, adolescent girls and women of reproductive age, pregnant women. A: The leading cause is dietary iron deficiency. B: The figures are 1.92 billion and 24.3%. C: Prevalence fell from 28.2% to 24.3%. D: Not the data given.

questions.stem: According to WHO 2024, which hemoglobin value defines anemia?

options.A: Below 10.5 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 11.5 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.B: Below 11.0 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 11.5 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.C: Below 10.5 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 12.0 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.D: Below 11.5 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 10.5 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.E: Below 10.0 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 11.0 g/dL at 5–11 years

questions.explanation: WHO 2024: 6–23 months <10.5; 24–59 months <11.0; 5–11 years <11.5; 12–14 years and non-pregnant women <12.0; men <13.0; pregnancy 1st and 3rd trimester <11.0, 2nd trimester <10.5. B: The 6–23 month cutoff was lowered to 10.5. C: 12.0 applies from 12 years. D: Reversed. E: Not the cutoffs.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has a hemoglobin of 6.0 g/dL. How is this graded by WHO 2024?

options.A: Moderate anemia (7.0–9.9 g/dL at 24–59 months)
options.B: Severe anemia (below 8.0 g/dL at 24–59 months)
options.C: Severe anemia (below 7.0 g/dL at 24–59 months)
options.D: Mild anemia (10.0–10.9 g/dL at 24–59 months)
options.E: Moderate anemia (8.0–10.9 g/dL at 5–11 years)

questions.explanation: At 24–59 months: anemia <11.0, mild 10.0–10.9, moderate 7.0–9.9, severe <7.0. From 5 years and in adults the severe cutoff is <8.0. A: 6.0 is below 7.0. B: The severe cutoff under 5 years is 7.0; 8.0 applies from 5 years. D: 6.0 is far below. E: She is in the 24–59 month group.

questions.stem: Which change did WHO make in 2024?

options.A: Altitude adjustment now starts at 1000 m
options.B: Altitude adjustment now starts at 500 m
options.C: The smoking adjustment was dropped
options.D: An adjustment for ethnicity was added
options.E: An adjustment for inflammation was added

questions.explanation: Changes: cutoff for 6–23 months lowered from 11.0 to 10.5; new second-trimester cutoff 10.5; altitude adjustment starts at 500 m (was 1000 m); smoking adjustment kept; no adjustment for ethnicity or inflammation. A: It was 1000 m and is now 500 m. C: It was kept. D: There is no adjustment for ethnicity. E: There is no adjustment for inflammation.

questions.stem: How should anemia be classified?

options.A: By MCV first, then by severity
options.B: By mechanism in adults and by MCV in children
options.C: By reticulocyte count in each case
options.D: By mechanism and by MCV together
options.E: By hemoglobin level and age

questions.explanation: Classify two ways at once: by mechanism (decreased production, premature destruction, increased loss) and by red cell size (microcytic <80, normocytic 80–100, macrocytic >100 fL), always looking for the underlying cause. A: Mechanism and size are considered together. B: Both are used at the same time. C: The two axes are mechanism and MCV. E: That defines anemia, not its class.

questions.stem: Which findings point specifically to iron deficiency among the symptoms of anemia?

options.A: Exertional dyspnea and tachycardia
options.B: Fatigue and headache
options.C: Pallor and cool skin
options.D: A flow murmur
options.E: Pica and glossitis

questions.explanation: Digestive: anorexia, nausea; pica and glossitis in iron deficiency. Other systems: fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia, flow murmur, pallor, impaired T-cell and macrophage function. A: General cardiorespiratory signs. B: General nervous system symptoms. C: General signs. D: A general sign of anemia.

questions.stem: A child with a hemoglobin of 5 g/dL from long-standing iron deficiency is playful and hemodynamically stable. Which determinant of severity explains this?

options.A: How low the hemoglobin is
options.B: The MCV
options.C: The reticulocyte count
options.D: How fast the hemoglobin fell
options.E: The patient's sex

questions.explanation: Severity depends on how low the Hb is, how fast it fell (slow-onset anemia can be well tolerated even at very low Hb) and comorbidities. A: The level is very low yet tolerated. B: Not a determinant listed. C: Not a determinant listed. E: Not a determinant listed.

questions.stem: Which simple labs complete the diagnostic approach after confirming anemia, history and examination?

options.A: CBC with indices, ferritin and bone marrow aspirate
options.B: CBC with indices, reticulocyte count and blood smear
options.C: Blood smear, hemoglobin electrophoresis and B12
options.D: Reticulocyte count, Coombs test and LDH
options.E: CBC with indices, lead level and CRP

questions.explanation: Approach: confirm anemia, focused history, thorough exam, simple labs (CBC and indices, reticulocyte count, blood smear). A: Not the first simple labs. C: Not the first simple labs. D: Not the first simple labs. E: Not the first simple labs.

questions.stem: In the family history of an anemic child, what does an early cholecystectomy in a relative suggest?

options.A: An inherited bleeding disorder in the family
options.B: Iron deficiency
options.C: Hemolysis with early gallstones
options.D: Marrow failure
options.E: Lead exposure

questions.explanation: Family history: early splenectomy or cholecystectomy (early gallstones suggest hemolysis), early hysterectomy (may suggest a bleeding disorder), autoimmune disease, consanguinity, ethnic origin. Patient history includes neonatal jaundice, dark urine, transfusions, lead, milk intake, pica. A: That is suggested by early hysterectomy. B: Not the association. D: Not the association. E: Not the association.

questions.stem: How are skin bleeding lesions classified by size?

options.A: Petechiae up to 2 mm; purpura 3–10 mm; ecchymosis over 1 cm
options.B: Petechiae 3–10 mm; purpura up to 2 mm; ecchymosis over 1 cm
options.C: Petechiae up to 2 mm; purpura over 1 cm; ecchymosis 3–10 mm
options.D: Petechiae up to 2 cm; purpura 3–10 cm; ecchymosis over 10 cm
options.E: Petechiae up to 5 mm; purpura 5–20 mm; ecchymosis over 5 cm

questions.explanation: Petechiae ≤2 mm (pinpoint, flat, non-blanching); purpura 3–10 mm; ecchymosis >1 cm; hematoma: raised, palpable collection of clotted blood. B: The first two are swapped. C: The last two are swapped. D: The units are wrong. E: Not the sizes given.

questions.stem: Which mouth findings are sought on examination of an anemic patient?

options.A: Gingival hypertrophy and thrush
options.B: Glossitis and angular cheilitis
options.C: Aphthous ulcers and leukoplakia
options.D: Macroglossia and dental caries
options.E: Petechiae of the palate and tonsillar exudate

questions.explanation: Mouth: glossitis (smooth, sore tongue) and angular cheilitis. Other signs: icterus, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, leg ulcers, abnormal facies. A: Not the findings listed. C: Not the findings listed. D: Not the findings listed. E: Not the findings listed.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a cause of microcytic anemia EXCEPT:

options.A: Thalassemia
options.B: Lead poisoning
options.C: Hypothyroidism
options.D: Sideroblastic anemia
options.E: Late anemia of inflammation

questions.explanation: Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassemia, late anemia of inflammation, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia. Hypothyroidism causes non-megaloblastic macrocytosis. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which causes of macrocytic anemia are non-megaloblastic?

options.A: Alcohol, liver disease and hypothyroidism
options.B: B12 deficiency, folate deficiency and alcohol
options.C: Folate deficiency, liver disease and lead poisoning
options.D: Alcohol, thalassemia and hypothyroidism
options.E: B12 deficiency, myelodysplasia and iron deficiency

questions.explanation: Macrocytic: megaloblastic (B12 or folate deficiency, drugs) and non-megaloblastic (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, drugs). B: B12 and folate deficiency are megaloblastic. C: Folate deficiency is megaloblastic; lead is microcytic. D: Thalassemia is microcytic. E: B12 is megaloblastic; iron deficiency is microcytic.

questions.stem: A patient has a normocytic anemia. How does the reticulocyte count direct the differential?

options.A: Low: hemorrhage or hemolysis; high: marrow failure; normal: early anemia of inflammation
options.B: Low: early anemia of inflammation; high: marrow failure; normal: hemolysis
options.C: Low: iron deficiency; high: thalassemia; normal: lead poisoning
options.D: Low: marrow failure; high: hemorrhage or hemolysis; normal: early anemia of inflammation
options.E: Low: marrow failure; high: B12 deficiency; normal: hemolysis

questions.explanation: Normocytic: low reticulocytes = marrow failure, ineffective erythropoiesis; high = hemorrhage or hemolysis (extrinsic immune/non-immune; intrinsic membrane, enzyme, hemoglobinopathy); normal = early anemia of inflammation. A: Low and high are swapped. B: Not the scheme. C: These are microcytic causes. E: Not the scheme.

questions.stem: To decide between production failure and increased destruction, which test is the most informative?

options.A: Mean corpuscular volume
options.B: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin
options.C: Blood smear
options.D: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
options.E: Reticulocyte count

questions.explanation: The reticulocyte count shows how active the marrow is: low in production failure, high in destruction or loss. A: It classifies size, not mechanism. B: Not the answer given. C: Helpful, but the count is the most informative here. D: Not the answer given.

questions.stem: Which ferritin threshold does ASH 2026 give for iron deficiency without inflammation?

options.A: ≤ 12 ng/mL in children; ≤ 15 ng/mL in adults
options.B: ≤ 30 ng/mL in children; ≤ 20 ng/mL in adults
options.C: ≤ 50 ng/mL in children; ≤ 100 ng/mL in adults
options.D: ≤ 20 ng/mL in children; ≤ 30 ng/mL in adults
options.E: ≤ 20 ng/mL at each age

questions.explanation: ASH 2026 (no inflammation): children 9 months–4 years and older children ≤20 ng/mL (previously ≤12); adults, menstruating and pregnant ≤30 (up to ≤50 with symptoms, risk factors or anemia in pregnancy; previously ≤15). A: These are the previous thresholds. B: Reversed. C: Not the thresholds. E: Adults use ≤ 30 (up to ≤ 50 with symptoms or risk factors).

questions.stem: How should the ASH 2026 ferritin thresholds be applied?

options.A: With inflammation use ferritin < 100 ng/mL or TSAT < 20%; a threshold prompts assessment
options.B: With inflammation in adults use ferritin < 30 ng/mL; a threshold mandates iron treatment
options.C: With or without inflammation the same threshold applies
options.D: Higher cutoffs carry no risk and rest on high-certainty evidence
options.E: With inflammation use TSAT > 45%

questions.explanation: The thresholds apply only without inflammation. With inflammation (adults): ferritin <100 ng/mL or TSAT <20%. A threshold prompts assessment, not automatic iron; higher cutoffs risk overdiagnosis and iron overload, especially in children; most evidence is low certainty. B: The inflammation criterion is <100 or TSAT <20%, and a threshold prompts assessment only. C: Thresholds apply only without inflammation. D: They risk overdiagnosis and iron overload; evidence is mostly low certainty. E: Not the criterion.

questions.stem: What did the 2026 NHANES analysis of children aged 5–14 show?

options.A: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 15 µg/L, lowering prevalence from 30% to 9%
options.B: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 100 µg/L in boys aged 5–7
options.C: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 24 µg/L, raising prevalence from 9% to 30%
options.D: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 24 µg/L, detected by reticulocyte count
options.E: Iron supply is normal until ferritin < 5 µg/L

questions.explanation: In 3,765 healthy US children, the ferritin level at which red cell iron supply first falters (by zinc protoporphyrin) was <24 µg/L: 30% iron deficient versus 9% with the old cutoff (about 15). Girls aged 12–14 were most affected. A: The physiologic cutoff is <24 and prevalence rises. B: Not the finding; girls 12–14 were most affected. D: It was identified with zinc protoporphyrin. E: Not the finding.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl, breastfed until 1 year and then fed mostly cow's milk, is markedly pale with Hb 6.0 g/dL, MCV 70 fL and normal white cells and platelets. What is the most likely cause, and what additional mechanism does cow's milk add?

options.A: Thalassemia trait; cow's milk blocks globin synthesis
options.B: Iron deficiency; cow's milk can cause occult blood loss
options.C: Lead poisoning; cow's milk contains lead
options.D: B12 deficiency; cow's milk lacks cobalamin
options.E: Anemia of inflammation; cow's milk triggers allergy

questions.explanation: Most likely nutritional iron deficiency from excess cow's milk with little solid food; cow's milk can also cause occult intestinal blood loss. A: The dietary history points to iron deficiency. C: Lead often coexists and is screened for, but is not the main cause here. D: That would be macrocytic. E: Not the picture described.

questions.stem: In that child, which results are expected before treatment, and how is the diagnosis confirmed?

options.A: High reticulocytes, spherocytes, normal RDW; ferritin ≤ 20 ng/mL with CRP
options.B: Low reticulocytes, target cells, normal RDW; hemoglobin electrophoresis
options.C: Low reticulocytes, pencil cells, high RDW; bone marrow aspirate
options.D: Normal reticulocytes, schistocytes, low RDW; ferritin ≤ 100 ng/mL
options.E: Low reticulocytes, pencil cells, high RDW; ferritin ≤ 20 ng/mL with CRP

questions.explanation: Expect a low reticulocyte count for the degree of anemia, hypochromic microcytic cells, pencil cells, high RDW and low Ret-He. Confirm with ferritin ≤20 ng/mL (ASH 2026), checking CRP for inflammation; screen for lead exposure. A: Reticulocytes are low and the cells hypochromic and microcytic. B: That would suggest thalassemia. C: Ferritin confirms the diagnosis. D: Not the expected findings.

questions.stem: After starting oral iron, limiting cow's milk and adding iron-rich foods, what response is expected?

options.A: A rising hemoglobin within 1–2 days, then reticulocytosis after a month
options.B: Reticulocytosis within about 1 week, then a rising hemoglobin within weeks
options.C: Reticulocytosis within about 1 day, with a normal hemoglobin by 1 week
options.D: No reticulocyte change; ferritin normal within a week
options.E: Reticulocytosis within about 1 week; iron can then be stopped

questions.explanation: Expect reticulocytosis within about 1 week and a rising Hb within weeks; continue iron to replete stores. A: Reticulocytes rise first. C: Too fast. D: Not the expected course. E: Iron is continued to replete stores.

questions.stem: In which situation are nucleated red cells on a blood smear a normal finding?

options.A: In adolescents
options.B: In pregnancy
options.C: In newborns
options.D: After exercise
options.E: At high altitude

questions.explanation: Nucleated red cells (normoblasts) are seen in hemolysis, marrow stress or infiltration, and are normal in newborns. A: Not normal at that age. B: Not stated as normal. D: Not stated as normal. E: Not stated as normal.
